Amazing work. I finally got to have a look, and I have a few changes to request: 1. `motion_blur_jitter_tiles` should not be an option, that is my bad. It should always be true. Without it the seams between tiles are obvious. 2. `motoin_blur_velocity_depth_test` is also a redundant setting, and should be true by default. Again, my bad. 3. `target_framerate`, `framerate_independent`, and `uncapped_independence` should be reintroduced, as they are key features that users thould be able to play with. 4. All of the motion separatiion setting, that is all of these should be exposed. Their purpose is not clear, and I take the blame for not communicating them clearly enough. They are actually a key feature that make our motion blur effect as powerful as it is. They allow for movement separation between the camera's movement, rotation, and object's movement, allowing users to configure the contribution of each to the final blur separately! The thresholds are also a cool feature that expand upon the separation, allowing you to configure a velocity threshold for the "activation" of blur for each of these components. This can yield granular control by the user to keep the game view crisp and blur free unless some extreme motions occur. Something like this: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/02fb83ad-ec16-4544-8d1d-2f20cad52dbf Since this can be a bit cumbersome to have 6 properties, and yield diminishing returns in terms of granularity, we can consider just having one set of lower and upper threshold parameters that would apply to all 3 components at the same time. Edit: We can maybe come up with clearer way to expose the framerate related settings. It is not clear what these do and would be hard to communicate through doc comments. Also there are a lot of redundant configurations with them, so I imagine some enum to represent common "framerate modes" Edit 2: For the framerate modes I am thinking: `NATIVE` - the blur is determined purely based on the framerate of the game (`final_intensity = intensity`) `MIN_FRAMERATE` - the blur is determined based on the framerate of the game, but below a minimum framerate limit the amount of blur to that framerate (so it is not abnoxious) (`final_intensity = intensity * min(1 / minimum_framerate, time_step) / time_step`) `FORCE_FRAMERATE` - the blur is determined based on a fixed framerate defined by the user, so even at higher framerate it will maintain the same amount of blur (overblurring, but more consistent). (`final_intensity = intensity / (target_framerate * time_step)`) For the latter 2 modes, a framerate property should be dynamically exposed.
I apologize for the bother, I should have been cleaner and clearer about the setup.

The original issue was that motion blur was too small and rotating the camera was the only way to reliably see any blur, and that is fixed. I think just like every graphics related effect and state, the blur should be agnostic to whether it is ran in the editor or not. The editor does not render unnecessary frames which is amazing, but I believe that at its current state, its logic of when to render and when to not just does not consider the behavior of the velocity buffer. The fact is that when the editor stops rendering as soon as the camera stops moving, it is stuck on an outdated velocity buffer. This means that any other effect like TAA that makes use of the velocity buffer would also have to work with outdated state of the buffer. What I am saying is that this issue is caused by a lack of consideration from the editor towards the natural behavior of the velocity buffer. 
An important realization to make is that this issue does not extend just to camera rotation, but any object movement that abruptly stops.
Basically, what the editor needs to do differently on its own, is render an extra frame after it deems the scene to be "stationary" again, to flush out all velocities in the velocity buffer. This does not need to be a responsibility of the motion blur. The motion blur just surfaced this issue.

One of the main reasons for a feature PR to be merged is that the feature cannot be implemented as a plugin or there are substantial compromises to implementing it as a plugin.

In the description, I see a mention that performance should be better with this PR compared to the plugin, but it would be good to see some real world and benchmark performance comparisons between this PR and the plugin to demonstrate how substantial the performance gains are. This will help validate that this PR is worth the long term maintenance cost.

It would also be good to have this PR's description list and detail any other improvements or benefits to having this feature added to Godot compared to what was possible with the plugin. These will, again, help demonstrate why the long term maintenance of the feature is truly required and cannot be handled by a plugin.

I noticed that my [previous comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/115027#issuecomment-3855492635) received a lot of confused emojis, so I understand that there might be some confusion about what I wrote. I'll provide some clarification:

I wrote that note from the perspective that is generally taken with all PRs in Godot. This process helps us ensure a high quality, bug-free, maintainable game engine in the long run and is why we ask "Is there a reason why this should be core and not an add-on in the asset library?" in the proposal template. I noticed that the proposal for this PR has notes about how this PR should be better than the existing plugin.

All that said, I was not aware that a decision may have been made to include a motion blur feature in the Godot engine without the need for a plugin. So assuming that this decision has been made, it is still important to verify the performance characteristics of this PR and any differences/improvements/etc. that have been made compared to the plugin. This not only gives validation that integrating the feature into the core engine is valuable, but also ensures that the quality and characteristics of this PR are as-expected.

So, regardless of the exact reasons, seeing some performance comparisons and details regarding any other improvements or benefits compared to the plugin this PR is based off of will still be extremely valuable in the review of this PR.

If others who are interested in this PR are able, it would be good to test this PR with your own project to see how it performs, etc. Once a bug, problem, or limitation has been merged into Godot it becomes much harder to fix later on, so lots of testing of PRs is always appreciated!

Regarding orbiting third-person cameras, that's a normal limitation/issue with built in "cancel camera rotation motion blur" options in engines. I don't quite remember if I discussed this in length on the MB workshop Discord channel or elsewhere but the proper solution for this is an API that can be called per frame where you as the user/developer can feed in a specific custom translation and rotation vector to be very specific about what motion blur you want canceled.

The responsibility would then lie on you to collect and build said vectors somehow, but the benefit is that you have perfect control over what motion blur exactly you want cancelled. You can now do things like, motion blur caused by user input is cancelled out, but motion blur caused by the world is not - i.e. if the user rotates the camera, there's no motion blur, but if the player stands on a rotating platform, the motion blur caused by the rotation of the platform is preserved. Ect ect.

But that's outside the scope of this PR and IMHO is a full on feature - meaning this will be a separate, significant PR done *after* the core motion blur feature PR is merged.

I also think, for this PR, we should be specific about bugs and issues of the MB implementation itself, and bugs and issues due to the pretty bad state of motion vectors in Godot right now. As long as the MB effect itself is doing things correctly with whatever motion vector data it's being fed, that's the scope of this PR. Any issues with the motion vectors themselves (and there are many!) should be fixed separately - it'll benefit the rest of the engine and other motion vector dependent effects (i.e. TAA) anyway.

The mbtest project had this configuration of the DOF on it: Which basically put everything in front of the camera beyond the far plane. I would like to point out this is not a practical usecase of the effect. The compositor version is ran before the DOF is applied, and the native version is ran after the DOF. So with the settings above: Just DOF: With compositor MB: With native MB: Because the native MB is applied after the DOF, it smears the already blurred DOF color, and the gradients are thrown off. However, the reason the compositor MB seems to work better here is due to the fact the DOF is configured to apply uniformly to everything, which is not a practical usecase. A more practical usecase would be setting the far plane to some value beyond the target of interest, in this case the cube: With these new settings: Just DOF: With compositor MB: With native MB: Now, at first glance, it seems that the compositor MB is on-par with the native MB, but that's not quite right. Because the compositor MB is applied before the DOF, the feathering which extends from the cube onto the background gets blurred with the background during the DOF pass, leading to the feathering to be less accurate than the native MB. This can be seen more obviously when the background is a darker color, and the DOF's intensity is increased to 0.3: Now compare that to the native MB: Now the question is which is more visually robust. Having the motion blur before or after? I think having the motion blur before is still the better approach. Seems that even under perfect conditions there are outline artifacts with the MB happening after. The worst case of the MB before seems to be more visually acceptable than the worst case of the MB after, with the feathering losing its accuracy when the moving subject is crisp and the background is DOF'ed. That worst case is also less likely to happen.
